title: Prepositions of position and movement
subtitle: across / over, along / through, above / over, below / under
summary: Choose between across and over, along and through, and above, over, below and under according to shape, contact and direction.

lesson.heading: across or over: the other side
lesson.text: We can use **across** or **over** to talk about a position on the other side of, or movement to the other side of, a road, bridge, border, river and so on.

examples.text: Antonio lives in the house **across** / **over** the road from ours.
Once she was **across** / **over** the border, she knew she would be safe.

left.label: over - reaching the other side of something high
left.text: Something higher than it is wide.
examples: He jumped **over** the fence into the garden.

right.label: across - a flat surface or an area
examples: He suddenly saw Eva **across** the room.

lesson.heading: all over, not all across
lesson.text: To mean 'to or in many different parts of an area' we prefer **all over** rather than *all across*. We commonly use **across**, or **right across** for emphasis.

examples.text: The disease has now spread **all over** the world.

left.label: along - following a line
left.text: A road, a river, a path, a beach.
examples: They walked **along** the footpath until they came to a small bridge.

right.label: through - a three-dimensional space
right.text: Things all around you, often from one side or end to the other.
examples: He pushed his way **through** the crowd of people to get to her.
She walked **through** the forest to get to her grandmother's house.
Compare: She spent a lot of her free time walking **in** the forest.

lesson.heading: above or over?
lesson.text: Either can say that one thing is at a higher level than another. We prefer **above** when one thing is not directly over the other. We use **over**, not above, when something covers something else and touches it, and usually for horizontal movement at a higher level.

examples.text: **Above** / **Over** the door was a sign saying, 'Mind your head'.
They lived in a village in the mountains **above** the lake.
The bird hovered just a few metres **above** / **over** the lake.
She put a quilt **over** the bed.
I saw the helicopter fly out **over** the water, near the fishing boat.

lesson.heading: below and under
lesson.text: **Below** is the opposite of above; **under** is the opposite of over, and the differences work the same way.

examples.text: It's hard to believe that there is a railway line **below** / **under** the building.
Her head was **below** the level of the table so nobody noticed her.
She hid the presents **under** a blanket.
examples.note: the blanket covers and touches them
horizontal movement at a lower level

lesson.heading: underneath and beneath
lesson.text: **Underneath** works as an alternative to *under* as a preposition of place. **Beneath** is sometimes used as a more formal alternative to *under* or *below*.

examples.text: She found the letter **underneath** a pile of newspapers.

lesson.text: Does it cover and touch? Use over / under. Is it simply at a higher or lower level, not directly in line? Use above / below.

exercises.prompt: After I'd finished work I walked ___ the car park to where Mona was waiting.
exercises.explanation: A car park is a flat area, so across.

exercises.prompt: The gate was locked so we had to climb ___ the wall.
exercises.explanation: A wall is higher than it is wide, so we reach the other side over it.

exercises.prompt: ___ the table I could see Oliver looking at his watch.
exercises.explanation: The table top is a flat surface, so we see someone across it.

exercises.prompt: He fell ___ the floor into the cellar below.
exercises.explanation: Through describes movement from one side of a space to the other.

exercises.prompt: Hotels have been built ___ the beach for about 25 kilometres.
exercises.explanation: The beach is a line to follow, so along.

exercises.prompt: He cycles thousands of miles each year all ___ the country.
exercises.explanation: All over is much more likely than 'all across' or 'all through'.

exercises.prompt: It took several minutes to walk ___ the corridor to the exit.
exercises.explanation: A corridor is both a line to follow (along) and an enclosed space you pass through.

exercises.statement: He slept with his wallet below his pillow.
exercises.explanation: He slept with his wallet under his pillow. The pillow covers and touches the wallet.

exercises.statement: He lived in a first-floor flat above a greengrocer's in Leyton.
exercises.explanation: Correct - and over is also possible here.

exercises.statement: When the police got to the car they found the driver slumped above the steering wheel.
exercises.explanation: They found the driver slumped over the steering wheel. He is touching it, so over.

exercises.prompt: Which preposition fits each gap: under or below?

items.text: He slept with his wallet ___ his pillow.
She hid the presents ___ a blanket.
He always wore a vest ___ his shirt, even in summer.
Her head was ___ the level of the table so nobody noticed her.
The town stood at the top of the hill, and stretching into the distance ___ it were green fields.

exercises.prompt: Match these idioms with their meanings.

pairs.left: I'm just feeling rather under the weather.
That's a bit below the belt, isn't it?
She has 18 books on gardening under her belt.
He had never played well for the club and left under a cloud.
She lost her temper and went completely over the top.
They received a bonus over and above their monthly salary.
